Lens items verified as holding:
- Verification-phase params: device answers judge the executor and every same-action verification check (respond candidate list), and planner restricts verification capability checks to READ contracts, so no write-class verification exists to smuggle.
- Calculator batches: device allow_batch requires cross-app consent naming every action (Agent) and remoteExecutionRefusal on every planned op of the covered actions; consultBatch matches exact operation digests per stepId, so a device batch covers only planned Calculator ops. Non-Calculator EXECUTE, terminal, skills and sensitive/hardApproval are refused.
- Agent consent: computer ops stay bound by agenticScopeViolation even with a one-time answer (only filesystem uses reviewedFilesystemOnce, the accepted disposition). Fingerprint and revision are checked for one-time Agent requests; crossAppInputs (content) changes the params so the fingerprint mismatches and the request asks again.
- Stale/superseded: respond() requires pendingRequestId == requestId; device answers refused for desktopRequired/remoteReview; expired or revoked envelopes refused at answer time and denied in decide for remote envelopes.
- approvedOnce across attempts: Retry clears it for non-completed steps; Host restart clears it for ready/running/verifying steps and denies pending requests; Stop makes the Mission non-retryable.
- Revocation: endDeviceAnswers, endDeviceDriven, batch and delegation revocation are wired in http.server.ts endDeviceGrants.
- Device route gates: mission.retry/replan/restart are not in DEVICE_RIGHTS (refused at HTTP); agent.authorization.approve on a waiting_for_approval mission is refused by deviceAgenticRefusal; reauthorize by a device creates a remote envelope (ceiling applies); direct task approve by device requires deviceMayLaunch; submit by device queues waiting_for_approval.

Non-exploitable observations (not reported as findings):
1. project.context device answers: candidate params skip scope checks (manager.server.ts ~2106). Reachable only for an Agent model step after CONTEXT_CHANGED. The answer only re-runs launch, and agenticProviderCheck revalidates the context (projectContext.revalidate), so no authority is gained; it is a retry past a context change the workstation has not reviewed.
2. The bus batch rescue in decision() (bus.server.ts ~180-200) does not check batch.createdBy, so a device-created batch can rescue ordinary asks on workstation envelopes. consultBatch's exact operation digests and the device planned-op check keep it to exact planned Calculator ops, which matches the owner policy.
3. The remoteMutationHeld exemption (manager.server.ts ~2400) matches the workstation one-time by action, not params. Only the step's own executor can be a held mutation (verification checks are READ), so no exploit path found.
4. Device allow_batch is never consulted on the agentic-violation path (isTrustedLocalActor gate). Availability only, not authority.
5. Accepted items observed (not re-reported): device one-time widening of Agent filesystem steps within the store envelope; workstation one-time after workstation envelope expiry; Git reads under remote authority with owner-configured filters.

findings.title: Paired-device command responses carry desktop grant, operation and binding records
findings.scenario: A paired device answers or stops a Mission (mission.respond, mission.approve, mission.start, mission.stop, mission.revoke_batch). Each of these returns missions.view(), which copies every request record raw (requests = store.requests(...).slice(0,20)). The stored record includes desktopOperation (absolute cwd, resolved executable path, file identities), desktopBinding (authorizationId, planReference, mutationSequence) and, after a workstation allow_once, desktopGrant (grant id, hostId, Host epoch, stepId, taskId, operation). The HTTP json() redaction (http.server.ts:131) only replaces strings matching review-listing text, so these keys pass through. Only /state (manager.server.ts:2169 remoteVerdicts) and mission.get (manager.server.ts:2241 deviceMissionData) strip them. Probed at manager/command level with the real MissionManager: device mission.respond deny on a terminal.exec desktop ask returned desktopOperation {cwd:"C:\\...\\project", executable:{file:"C:\\Program Files\\nodejs\\node.exe"}} and desktopBinding {authorizationId, planReference, mutationSequence:0}. After a workstation allow_once on an earlier request, the device's next respond response included the full desktopGrant record (grant id, hostId, epoch, operation). Policy says a paired device sees the desktop-required flag, never grant or exact-operation records. No authority is gained: the Host takes only requestId and decision from a device, and grant ids are never accepted from the client.
findings.evidence: Probe script (mkdtemp under OS temp, deleted afterwards). Output: 'device respond response contains desktopOperation true', 'contains desktopBinding true', 'leaked cwd: C:\\Users\\...\\project | executable: {"file":"C:\\Program Files\\nodejs\\node.exe"}'. Second probe: 'device sees answered workstation request desktopGrant: {"id":"26dd6b24-...","requestId":...,"hostId":...,"epoch":...,"stepId":...}'. Code: commands.server.ts:52,61,63,78 return {mission: missions.view(...)} or the respond result; manager.server.ts:521-535 view(); http.server.ts:131 json(); manager.server.ts:2169 and 2241 strip only in /state and mission.get.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same device projection to every device-facing mission view. Strip desktopGrant, desktopOperation and desktopBinding in view() when the caller is a device, or route the command responses through deviceMissionData. Add a regression test that asserts absence of these keys in mission.respond, mission.approve, mission.start and mission.stop responses to a device.

findings.title: Device mission.get events name trusted-desktop grant ids and the Host epoch
findings.scenario: The workstation's allow_once on a desktop-required ask emits approval.desktop_grant with the grant id, request id and Host epoch. Later uses emit approval.desktop_grant_used, and revocation emits approval.desktop_grant_revoked. Mission events are returned in mission.get (missionEvents slice). deviceMissionData (manager.server.ts:2241) redacts only review-listing text via redactReviewListing, so these grant-record details reach the device. Probed: a device's mission.get returned approval.desktop_grant ('Trusted-desktop grant 26dd6b24-... for request 7cb5bd5d-...: terminal.exec; single use until ... in Host epoch e8933b2c-...') and approval.desktop_grant_used ('... used (1/1) for terminal.exec'). This is the same policy gap as the command-response finding (grant records visible to a device), without authority gain.
findings.evidence: Probe output 'device mission.get events naming grants: [approval.desktop_grant: Trusted-desktop grant 26dd6b24-... ; approval.desktop_grant_used: ... used (1/1) for terminal.exec.]'. Emit sites: manager.server.ts:3721 (approval.desktop_grant), plus approval.desktop_grant_used in consumeDesktopGrant and approval.desktop_grant_revoked in revokeDesktopGrants. Device SSE path (http.server.ts publicEventDetail) does replace details, so only mission.get is affected.
findings.recommendation: Filter or generalise the approval.desktop_grant* event details in the device projection (deviceMissionData or the event projection), the same way SSE details are replaced with publicEventDetail. Keep the full text in workstation-visible events only.

result.reasoning: The finding's technical claim holds on static reading; I did not run any probe or test. The device-facing command responses are built from raw view(): manager.server.ts:500-540 copies every request record (`requests = store.requests(...).slice(0,20)`) without stripping desktopOperation, desktopBinding or desktopGrant. The commands that return view() to a device include mission.start (commands.server.ts:61), mission.respond (manager.server.ts:3642 and the respond path), mission.approve, mission.stop and revoke_batch. http.server.ts:131-133 json() applies redactReviewListing only when DEVICE_RESPONSES has the response, and authorization.server.ts:159-166 redacts only strings matching REVIEW_TEXT and never removes keys. So the keys pass through. The stripping exists only in remoteVerdicts (manager.server.ts:2169) and deviceMissionData (manager.server.ts:2244), which is an inconsistency with the code's own stated invariant ("a paired device sees the desktop-required flag, never grant or exact-operation records"). Impact is limited. No authority is gained: mission.respond accepts only requestId, decision, maxActions and ttlMs (commands.server.ts line for mission.respond), and the grant is read only from stored records (manager.server.ts ~2294-2306), so a leaked grant id is never accepted back. The leaked fields are metadata: resolved executable path and prefix, file digests for terminal.exec, operation digest, grant id, envelope id, planReference and mutationSequence. The absolute mission root already reaches devices in /state, because the ...mission spread in remoteVerdicts keeps `root`. This is not an owner-policy disposition and not an accepted limitation, so I do not refute it. I rate it LOW rather than MEDIUM: it is a real projection gap that breaks a stated invariant, but it exposes no secret and no authority.

The finding is real but overstated. I re-read the paths and did not run a probe or the test suite.

Confirmed in code:
- manager.server.ts:521-534 view() copies every request raw (desktopOperation, desktopBinding, desktopGrant are stored on the record via saveRequest at 3711-3713 and 3691).
- respond() (3644-3700s) returns this.view(...) and mission.respond/approve/start/stop/revoke_batch return view(), so a device gets the raw records in commands.server.ts:52,61,63,78,81.
- http.server.ts:131 json() redacts only strings matching REVIEW_TEXT (authorization.server.ts:157), which does not match the operation/binding/grant keys. http.server.ts:397 marks device responses, so the redaction runs but does not strip these keys.
- Only remoteVerdicts (manager.server.ts:2167-2169, used by /state at http.server.ts:342) and deviceMissionData (2241-2244, used by mission.get) strip them. deviceMissionData's own doc comment says a device may see "no grant, exact-operation or binding records", and remote-authority.test.ts:800 asserts that for mission.get only. The command responses are untested, so the code's own stated contract is violated there.

Why not higher: no authority is gained. The Host accepts only requestId, decision, maxActions and ttlMs from a device (commands.server.ts:66-78), grant ids are never read from client input (grep shows no client path into desktopGrant/consume), and grant consumption is Host-internal. The disclosed data is absolute cwd, resolved executable path, mutation sequence, authorization id, plan reference and the grant id. That is an information leak to an already paired device, not code execution or action outside the envelope.

Related gap the finding did not name: the 'approval.desktop_grant' event (manager.server.ts:3719-3722) carries the grant id, action and epoch. deviceMissionData passes events through unfiltered (only requests are mapped), and "Trusted-desktop" does not match REVIEW_TEXT, so mission.get events likely expose it too. Not probed. capability.run (commands.server.ts:89-92) returns the bus outcome, which can include desktopOperation, which is the same class of leak. Not probed.

Recommendation stands: project the command responses through deviceMissionData or strip the three keys in view() for device callers, and add the regression test. Severity LOW, since it is a policy-consistency leak with no authority.

findings.title: Python task check fails with an approval message but raises no review prompt
findings.scenario: A paired device writes a planned .txt file (device one-time answer or device-driven Mission), so pendingRemoteChanges() is non-empty. A workstation Mission whose step carries a Python task_spec verification then runs its check. TaskManager sets verification to {passed:false} with the 'Approval required on Windows Host ... before a Python check runs' text and no request is created, so the Task fails. Bounded retries and reroutes repeat the same failure. Only MissionManager.respond() acknowledges pending changes, and that runs only when some other code run produces an ask. This path therefore offers the workstation no way to clear the hold from the failing Mission.
findings.evidence: manager.server.ts:1463-1466 (held => passed:false, no askPermission/ask path, state=failed). src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:179 supplies the text via codeRunGate. acknowledgeRemoteChanges is called only in respond(). remote-authority.test.ts F01-R53 asserts only codeRunGate() text, not the Task outcome or an ask. Not end-to-end probed.
findings.recommendation: Make a held Python check raise a desktop-required review ask (with remoteReview ids from pendingRemoteReview) instead of a silent failed verification, or document that the workstation must run another code step to clear the hold and say so in the failure text.

findings.title: Survivor watcher drops descendants whose creation time is unreadable (fail-open)
findings.scenario: After a session's root exits, watchSurvivors keeps lineage members only when row.createdAt equals the recorded birth time, and skips any unseen row whose createdAt is null. A live descendant whose creation time Windows does not report (process-tree.server.ts:14 yields createdAt null when CreationDate is empty) is therefore never counted as live code. liveCodeExecutions() then reports no live code and a paired-device change is not held while that workstation-approved process still runs. Requires Windows to return no CreationDate for a live descendant, which is rare.
findings.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors with stubbed db/readProcesses): control with child createdAt=2000 tracks pid 101; child with createdAt=null after root exit tracks nothing; child never sampled with createdAt=null is never discovered. manager.server.ts:1730 and :1735 are the two conditions.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed for unknown creation times: keep a lineage member alive when its createdAt is null, and treat an unseen row with a live lineage parent as a descendant even when its createdAt is null (or refuse the paired-device hold window when any descendant's creation time is missing).

findings.title: Review listings JSON-encode path names but do not escape bidi or line-separator characters
findings.scenario: The review listing line is built from JSON.stringify(path) with no bidi escaping, unlike describeRemoteChange's content preview (manager.server.ts:81). A path containing U+202E or U+2066-2069 can reorder the text that follows it on the workstation prompt. Paths are the planned step's paths, not device-chosen, so a device cannot exploit this. It only conflicts with the stated (H)/(U) escaping claim.
findings.evidence: Probe: JSON.stringify('invoice‮fdp.txt') keeps the raw U+202E in the listing line (checked with node). The same unescaped path encoding appears at manager.server.ts:2413 (remoteMutationHeld target) and :3495 (askPermission deviceChanges).
findings.recommendation: Run path names through the same bidi/line-separator escape used for content previews, at every site that prints paths into prompts (lines 2348, 2413, 3495).

result.reasoning:
Refutation attempt failed; the defect is real but is information disclosure only, with no authority gain.

Checked:
- manager.server.ts:540 puts `events: this.store.missionEvents(id).slice(-200)` into the Mission view, so approval.desktop_grant / _used / _revoked records are in the view.
- commands.server.ts:80 returns `missions.deviceMissionData(view)` for devices. deviceMissionData (manager.server.ts:2241-2246) strips desktopGrant, desktopOperation and desktopBinding from requests only. It never touches `events`.
- redactReviewListing (authorization.server.ts:159-170) matches only "under paired-device authority", "paired-device change" or "a paired-device <x> of". Grant event text ("Trusted-desktop grant <uuid> for request <uuid>: ...; single use until ... in Host epoch ...") does not match, so it passes through unredacted.
- The SSE path does replace details (http.server.ts:448 uses publicEventDetail), so only mission.get is affected, as the finding says.

Why it is LOW and not higher:
- No device input accepts a grant id. mission.respond accepts only requestId/decision/maxActions/ttlMs, and grant consumption is server-side from the Host-held request record. The grant id is not a credential.
- The Host epoch is already exposed to devices: hostIdentity is served in the state payload (http.server.ts:340) and in operation status responses (http.server.ts:583-584). Epoch disclosure is not new.
- request.id and the action name (e.g. terminal.exec) are already visible to devices in mission.get requests. The new facts are the grant id, the expiry, and use counts.
- The owner policy does not list grant metadata as forbidden to devices.

It is still a real inconsistency: deviceMissionData's own docstring says "no grant, exact-operation or binding records", and the event log leaks grant records the projection was meant to hide. Recommended fix matches the finding.

Probe: no probe run. The conclusion rests on code reading of the paths above. The repo was not modified, and the test file was not run.

Not refuted. The finding is real and matches the code.

Code path confirmed:
- commands.server.ts:80 serves mission.get to devices as `missions.deviceMissionData(view)`.
- manager.server.ts:536-547 `get()` returns `events: this.store.missionEvents(id).slice(-200)`, and deviceMissionData (manager.server.ts:2241-2246) spreads `data`, so events pass through unchanged. It only strips desktopGrant/desktopOperation/desktopBinding from requests.
- The redaction regex in authorization.server.ts:157 (`under paired-device authority|paired-device change|a paired-device [\w.]+ of `) does not match the grant text "Trusted-desktop grant <uuid> for request <uuid>: terminal.exec; single use until ... in Host epoch ...", so redactReviewListing leaves it intact.
- Emit sites: manager.server.ts:3719-3724 (approval.desktop_grant), 2435-2439 (approval.desktop_grant_used), 2464 (approval.desktop_grant_revoked).
- The SSE path does replace details (http.server.ts:448, publicEventDetail), so the leak is specific to mission.get. This is inconsistent with the documented intent at manager.server.ts:2240 ("no grant, exact-operation or binding records" for a device).

Authority check: no device-facing input accepts a grant id. desktopCapabilityGrant (2302-2310) and desktopSessionGrant (2292-2296) look up grants from stored request records, and the bus gets its grant id from the Host callback (bus.server.ts:174-177, 299-300), not from request params. The grant id therefore cannot be replayed by a device. The exposed data is the grant UUID, the request id (already visible to devices in requests), the action name, the expiry and the Host epoch (manager.instanceId, also returned in operation-status responses at http.server.ts:583-584). None of this is an authority gain, and no owner-policy disposition or accepted limitation covers it. Severity LOW (information disclosure, contrary to the stated device projection contract) is fair; INFO would also be defensible.

Not probed further beyond code reading: the finding's own probe output is consistent with this path. No repo files were edited and no tests were run. test-results/ shows no changes from me.

Verified against the code:
- src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1463-1466: for a python check, `held = this.codeRunGate?.() ?? null`; if held, `verification = { passed: false, detail: held }` and state becomes "failed" with error "Bunny-A verification failed: ...". No askPermission or request is created on this path. The detail text begins with DESKTOP_REQUIRED ("Approval required on Windows Host ..."), so the user is told approval is needed when no approval request exists.
- src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:179 wires codeRunGate to pendingRemoteReview(), which is host-wide. The gate is correct as a fail-closed control: it does not let a device cause code execution.
- acknowledgeRemoteChanges is called only at manager.server.ts:3716, inside respond() for allow_once by a trusted local actor. The workstation can therefore clear the hold through any other review-carrying ask: a runsCode, git.*, github.*, or shell-capable session ask carries remoteReview ids (bus.server.ts:169-170, manager.server.ts:1472, 2054), and the answer acknowledges the shown ids. So the claim of "no way to clear" is overstated: the hold clears only through an unrelated code-run ask, which a Mission whose only code run is the check never produces.
- Retry path (manager.server.ts:1299) re-runs the same gate, so a Mission with only this check stays blocked until that other ask appears.
- Test F01-R53 (remote-authority.test.ts:1567) asserts only the codeRunGate() text, not the Task outcome or an ask, as the finding says.

Not a security issue: the device still cannot cause execution. It is a correctness/availability defect (misleading "approval required" text with no approval path). Not one of the listed dispositions or accepted limitations. Severity LOW fits.

So the failing Mission has no in-band way out, but the workstation can unblock via another code run. findings.title: Survivor watcher dedupe keyed by Task id and root PID skips a later attempt whose root reuses the PID (mid-run hold fails open)
findings.scenario: A Task runs attempt 1 with root PID 1234 and child 5678; both exit and the tree-cleanup tick deletes the lingering entry. A retry (attempt 2) of the same Task gets root PID 1234 again (Windows reuses freed PIDs) and spawns a child that outlives its root. watchSurvivors(id, 1234) returns early because survivorRoots.get(id) === 1234, so no watcher is created for attempt 2. liveCodeExecutions() then reports nothing for that surviving workstation-approved process, so remoteMutationHeld() does not hold a paired-device filesystem.write while that code is still running. Probed with the real TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors on a stub process table: after attempt 1 cleanup, attempt 2's child alive (pid 5678, born 301) gives lingering entries [] and 'hold would see live code' = false.
findings.evidence: Probe (throwaway, deleted): snapshot [{1234,born 100},{5678,born 101}] watched, rows emptied, 10.6 s tick -> []; then watchSurvivors('task-A',1234) with rows [{1234,born 300}] root exited and child {5678,ppid 1234,born 301} alive -> tracked entries after next tick: []. Dedupe at manager.server.ts:1715-1716 (survivorRoots.set(id, rootPid)); lingering watcher keyed only by id#n. Attempts are keyed by Task id, not by attempt, and the dedupe never compares createdAt.
findings.recommendation: Dedupe per attempt, not per numeric PID: key survivorRoots by rootPid plus the root's createdAt (from the session's processTree snapshot or a fresh readProcesses row), or clear survivorRoots[id] when a new attempt launches (relaunch and launch paths). Add a regression test: same root PID across two attempts of one Task with a surviving child must produce a live lingering entry.

findings.title: remoteActorFor fails open: a read error returns null, so a device-authored mutation is neither recorded nor held
findings.scenario: remoteActorFor() returns null when the answered-request lookup throws (catch at line 2334). remoteMutationStarted() then records no pending change, and remoteMutationHeld() does not hold the write, even though the Mission was device-driven or a device answered it. Policy requires unknown classification to fail closed. Reachable only when the store read throws (corrupt or unreadable record); not device-triggerable in normal operation. The review gate itself is unaffected for changes already recorded.
findings.evidence: manager.server.ts:2319-2334: the try around this.store.requests(...).find(...) ends with catch { return null; }; the deviceDriven try at 2323-2325 falls through rather than failing closed. Code read only, not probed.
findings.recommendation: On exception in the attribution lookup, return a fail-closed actor such as 'unknown-device' (treated as remote for recording and holds), not null.

findings.title: Superseded Agentic review re-ask reuses the ask-time reason and listing instead of rebuilding from the current listing
findings.scenario: reissueStaleAgenticRequests() closes an open desktop review ask after an Agentic revision change and re-asks it with request.reason (the old listing text, old sha256 and content) and the old remoteReview ids. The DesktopRequestStale path (around line 3698-3710) rebuilds the reason from pendingRemoteReview(); this path does not, so the workstation can be shown and approve file content that changed after the original ask. The approval acks only the old record ids; newer changes stay pending and any code run still re-asks, so no unreviewed code executes. The defect is in the approval prompt's integrity, not an execution bypass, and it contradicts the round-10 (F) intent for this path.
findings.evidence: Code read only. Path: reissueStaleAgenticRequests (manager.server.ts:2472) -> askPermission(..., request.reason, ..., request) at line 2493. Contrast: line 3698-3702 uses pendingRemoteReview() and request.reason.split(...) only when no review applies.
findings.recommendation: For requests with remoteReview, rebuild reason and remoteReview from pendingRemoteReview() in the reissue path, as the DesktopRequestStale path does, and keep the old ids only when they still match the current listing.

result.reasoning:
The defect is real but narrower than the finding states, and it is not an owner-policy disposition or accepted limitation (the accepted "persistently failing read stays held" case is fail-closed, this one fails open).

Code: manager.server.ts:1730 keeps a lineage member whose recorded birth is null (`born === null` => alive), so a null-createdAt descendant that a tree sample saw before the root exited IS tracked. The finding's "sampled null child tracks nothing" claim is therefore wrong. Line 1735 (`row.createdAt === null` => continue) is the real gap: a descendant that no sample ever recorded and that first appears after the root exits is never added to lineage, so liveCodeExecutions() (missions manager.server.ts ~2395-2400) reports nothing for it and remoteMutationHeld() (~2411) does not hold the paired-device change.

Probe (throwaway temp folder, deleted afterwards; TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors called with stubbed db/readProcesses, root pid 101 exited):
- child sampled before exit, createdAt set: tracked [102]
- child sampled before exit, createdAt null: tracked [102] (not a gap)
- child never sampled, createdAt null, first seen after exit: tracked [] (gap reproduced)
- child never sampled, createdAt set: tracked [102]

Preconditions: Windows must return no CreationDate (process-tree.server.ts:14 via the empty-CreationDate branch) for a live Bunny-launched descendant that no 2-15 s tick captured before the root exited. A device cannot influence CreationDate or sampling timing, so this is not a device-to-execution path; it is a fail-open availability/defence-in-depth gap. A related wider gap: processTable on non-Windows (process-tree.server.ts:18) sets createdAt null on every row, which disables discovery of any post-exit descendant. The Host's Codex Mission profile and Computer runtime are Windows-only, so this is secondary. Severity LOW is appropriate; the recommendation (fail closed for null creation times) matches the owner's fail-closed policy.

Not refuted. The mechanism reproduces as claimed. I read manager.server.ts:1714-1745 (watchSurvivors). Line 1730 keeps a lineage member only when its born value is null/undefined or equals the current createdAt. Line 1735 skips any unseen row whose createdAt is null, so a null-creation-time descendant that appears after the last 15 s tree snapshot is never discovered. process-tree.server.ts:10 and :14 confirm createdAt becomes null when Win32_Process.CreationDate is empty.

Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, watchSurvivors.call on a stub with db, readProcesses and lingering maps; temp folder deleted afterwards):
- control, child in snapshot with createdAt 2000 and still 2000: tracked [101]
- A, child unseen, createdAt 2000 after root exit: tracked [101]
- B, child unseen, createdAt null after root exit: not tracked []
- C, child in snapshot with 2000, now null: not tracked []
- D, child in snapshot with null, still null: tracked [101]

So B and C are dropped, and the hold in remoteMutationHeld (bunny-missions manager.server.ts:2383-2411, via liveCodeExecutions) then sees no live code. The device cannot induce the null creation time itself. Reaching it needs a workstation-approved child whose CreationDate is unreadable to the Host, for example a cross-user child started by CreateProcessWithLogonW, and that child must first appear after the last snapshot. Impact is a paired-device write being read by running workstation-approved code before review, which is the invariant the hold text states. That is fail-open but narrow, so LOW. Not an owner-policy disposition or accepted limitation, since the accepted list covers untracked orphans and snapshot limits, not null creation times for tracked descendants. Related note, not separately reported: on non-win32 processTable (process-tree.server.ts:17-18) every row has createdAt null, so discovery never runs there. The Host is Windows-only (killProcess refuses other platforms), so this is out of scope.

Confirmed, not refuted. The dedupe is at src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1715-1716: `if (!rootPid || this.survivorRoots.get(id) === rootPid) return;` followed by `survivorRoots.set(id, rootPid)`. survivorRoots is only ever set (lines 82, 1715-1716) and never cleared, so any later attempt of the same Task id whose root PID equals the previous root PID gets no lingering watcher. The retry loop (around line 1431) and the finally block (line 1654) both call watchSurvivors with the same id, so a retry or reroute of one Task shares the key. The probe ran the real TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors on a stubbed object in a mkdtemp folder (deleted afterwards). Attempt 1 (root 1234, child 5678 born 101) produced a lingering key task-A#1, which was cleared to [] on the 10 s tick. Attempt 2 (root 1234 reused, child 5678 born 301 alive) produced survivorRoots [['task-A',1234]] and no lingering key at all, so liveCodeExecutions() would not report the surviving approved process and remoteMutationHeld() would not hold a paired-device write. None of the owner-policy dispositions or accepted limitations covers this: the accepted "orphans between tree samples" item concerns a different gap, and the Windows PID reuse is not listed. Likelihood is low: it needs the exact same root PID within one Task id, a surviving grandchild of the second attempt, and a device write that this code later consumes. The impact is a fail-open mid-run hold, which the round-4 contract requires to fail closed, so MEDIUM is the right severity. The Host-wide review gate still stops new code from starting while a change is unacknowledged, so the exposure is limited to already-running code. No repo files were edited and no repo tests were run; test-results/ was not touched.

Not on the accepted list: the accepted items cover intermediate-parent exits between samples and in-memory tracking across Host restarts, not per-Task PID dedupe. Impact is bounded: it is a fail-open of the mid-run hold (device data written while workstation code runs may be read unreviewed). It does not give a paired device code or shell execution, because remote writes are limited to data types and the Host-wide review gate still blocks any code run that starts later. The trigger needs a same-Task retry whose root PID matches the previous root (plausible on Windows PID reuse) plus a surviving child. Medium is the honest severity for a verified fail-open of a designed control with narrow preconditions. The reviewer's suggested fix (key the dedupe on rootPid plus createdAt, or clear survivorRoots[id] on each new attempt) is sound. Code read confirmed the fail-open shape, so the finding is not refuted. Verified in src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:2319-2335: remoteActorFor() returns null when the try around this.store.requests(missionId).find(...) throws (catch at 2334). The deviceDriven try at 2323-2325 also falls through on a read error. The fail-open is real as read. In src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:2319-2334, the deviceDriven try (2322-2326) falls through on error, and the answered-request try (2330-2334) ends in `catch { return null; }`. remoteMutationStarted (line 181-186) returns without calling store.recordRemoteChange when actor is null, and remoteMutationHeld (line 2403) returns null before any hold. So a store read throw during the lookup leaves a device-attributed mutation unrecorded and unheld. The bus (capabilities/bus.server.ts:307) calls remoteMutationStarted only after store.saveRun has committed, so the mutation proceeds once the lookup fails. Not refuted: this is a fail-open in a classification path, which the owner policy says must fail closed.

Why LOW and not higher: I found no device-reachable trigger. store.requests (store.server.ts:178) and store.mission use parameterized SQL, and the JSON it parses was written by JSON.stringify (store.server.ts:171), so it always parses. The find predicate (2332) only reads resolvedBy strings produced by server code. Reaching the catch needs a local SQLite read/IO fault or on-disk corruption, which already implies local disk access. The read has to fail while the same database's saveRun write succeeds, which is unlikely in practice. The finding's own scope matches this. I did not probe it: the fall-through is unambiguous from the code, and I ran no repo tests and changed no files. No test-results files changed.

Suggested fix as the finding says: on an exception in the attribution lookup, return a fail-closed marker (for example a device actor placeholder) so the change is recorded and held. Alternatively, let the error propagate so the mutation aborts.

Not refuted. The defect is real but it is a prompt-integrity/correctness issue with no execution path (LOW, as claimed).

Confirmed by code reading (no files written, no tests run, no probes needed):
- manager.server.ts:2472-2500 (reissueStaleAgenticRequests): askPermission is called with request.reason (line 2493) and the whole old request as the desktop argument (carrying the old remoteReview ids). No rebuild from pendingRemoteReview(), unlike the DesktopRequestStale path at 3698-3705, which does rebuild and was the round-10 (F) fix. (F) was therefore only applied to the mutation-sequence re-ask, not to the agentic-revision reissue.
- askPermission (3459-3495) only appends a path-only suffix of current remote changes (up to 12) to the old reason, so the prompt mixes the old listing (old sha256/content) with current paths. The workstation can see stale content for a file that has since changed.
- Store (store.server.ts:154-163): every change is a new row with its own id, so a rewrite of the same path adds a new pending row. Acknowledging the old ids leaves the new row pending.
- Execution re-checks the gate: capabilities/bus.server.ts:169 calls remoteReviewFor (pendingRemoteReview) inside decision() before any grant (line 174-177) and before grant consumption (line 300). The execution path recomputes decision at call time, so a code/git/github run after the reissued allow_once re-asks with the current listing. The provider path (manager.server.ts:1453) also recomputes review. The Python check path fails closed through codeRunGate (line 179). So no unreviewed code runs.

Secondary note that strengthens the finding slightly: the reissued grant binds the mutation sequence captured at reissue time (askPermission's desktopBinding), not at the original ask, so a change made between the original ask and the reissue does not supersede it. The review gate still blocks execution, so this is not a bypass, but it departs from the stated grant-binding contract.

Recommendation stands: rebuild reason and remoteReview from pendingRemoteReview() on this path (keeping old ids only when they still match), as the 3698 path does.

Verified by code reading only (no repo files edited, no tests run, nothing probed):
- reissueStaleAgenticRequests (manager.server.ts:2472-2497) re-asks with request.reason and passes the whole old request as the desktop argument (askPermission call at 2488). It never calls pendingRemoteReview(). The DesktopRequestStale path (3698-3705) does rebuild from the current listing, so the round-10 (F) intent is not applied to this path. The finding's line 2493 is the tail of that call; the call starts at 2488.
- The stale reason carries the ask-time listing: sha256, size and content (review listing built at manager.server.ts:2340-2350 and embedded in the provider.execute reason at ~1453-1470 and ~3789).
- askPermission (3493-3495) appends a current path list from remoteChanges() when desktopRequired, so the reissued prompt mixes stale content with current path names that have no content shown. Its reason can also repeat the "Files changed ... under paired-device authority" suffix, since the old reason already carries it.
- The approval only acknowledges the old ids (3715-3716). New writes are not covered: recordRemoteChange (store.server.ts:154-157) inserts a new row per write with no dedupe, and the bus records it before the adapter runs (manager.server.ts:183-187). Any row still unacknowledged keeps pendingRemoteReview() non-null.
- That host-wide gate is enforced at launch for shell-capable sessions (manager.server.ts:125, which runs for every phase including "launch"), for Python checks (line 179, codeRunGate), and through the bus remoteReviewFor (line 178). So a device write between ask and answer cannot run code without a fresh ask that shows its content.

Therefore no unreviewed code executes. The impact is that the workstation may approve a prompt whose content and path list do not match the acknowledged rows, plus a duplicated suffix. This is not covered by any listed disposition, so it is not refuted. Fix as recommended: rebuild reason and remoteReview from pendingRemoteReview() when remoteReview is non-empty, and strip the old suffix as 3703 does.
